overview: This 254-page file documents U.S. wartime and immediate postwar scrutiny of Japanese communities and activities across Latin America. Its core is the FBI’s secret 1945 monograph “The Japanese in Latin America,” a country-by-country survey linking migration, agricultural colonization, commerce, community associations, schools, religion, propaganda, diplomacy, and alleged intelligence or subversive networks. Supplementary FBI and State Department correspondence from 1944–46 investigates particular organizations, firms, individuals, aliases, address books, and clandestine communications in Mexico and South America, while also recording cultural-information efforts and the circulation of the monograph. Maps, photographs, demographic and trade statistics, organizational charts, wartime documents, Japan’s surrender instruments, and an index complete the file.
interest: The file is unusually useful because it combines granular investigative records with a synthetic, continent-wide intelligence assessment, allowing historians to compare case-level evidence with the broader conclusions officials drew from it. It offers extensive information on Japanese Latin American communities, businesses, institutions, and transnational connections, but it is equally revealing about U.S. security assumptions, racialized suspicion, and the production of wartime knowledge. Its descriptions of surveillance, internment, deportation, property controls, propaganda, and clandestine communications make it valuable for studying both diaspora history and inter-American wartime policy, provided its many allegations are treated critically rather than as established fact.
